title: Critical Vocabulary in Action
welcome_lead: Spot the techniques in real GCSE texts — and name them accurately under exam pressure.
meta_desc: GCSE English Literature — applying critical vocabulary to extracts from set texts.
final_note: You practised spotting pathetic fallacy, sibilance, dramatic irony, anachronism and zoomorphism in context.

walkthroughs.body_html:
In Macbeth, the night of Duncan's murder has 'the obscure bird' and chimneys 'blown down.'

Nature itself convulses to mirror the moral chaos. That is pathetic fallacy, a term coined by Ruskin.

Mr Birling calls the Titanic 'unsinkable' and says war is impossible.

The 1945 audience knows both predictions are catastrophically wrong. Priestley uses dramatic irony to demolish Birling's authority before the Inspector even speaks.

In Bayonet Charge the soldier 'plunged past with his bayonet toward the green hedge / King, honour. / Dropped like luxuries.'

He becomes 'a yellow hare' — zoomorphism. The animal image shows raw fear has stripped him of human ideals.

options: A pitiful argument
Weather reflecting mood
Comic exaggeration
An old-fashioned word

mcqs.q: Birling's claim the Titanic is 'unsinkable' is an example of which technique?
options: Sibilance
Pathetic fallacy
Dramatic irony
Anachronism
Pathetic fallacy is when characters cry over silly things.
When the audience knows something a character does not, creating tension between the character's words/actions and the audience's understanding.
Dramatic irony is when characters speak in dramatic voices.
Dramatic irony is when something ironic happens in a play.

mcqs.q: Why must students distinguish the narrator from the author?
options: The narrator and author are different words for the same thing.
The narrator is a constructed voice within the text; the author is the real person who created it. Conflating them misreads irony, unreliable narration and persona.
Pathetic fallacy is when characters cry over silly things.
The narrator's views are always the author's views.
